## EXISTING piepline

This pipeline was used for progress report 2, it has been updated to reflect the final analysis

## Prereqs

In addition to tidyverse packages, `corrplot`, `mda.biber`, `spacyr`, `udpipe`, and `quanteda` will all need to be installed. 

Additionally, an installation of python (3.10+) is required to utilize spaCy R. Once these are installed, everything can be completed within R as described below. 

[Information on spaCy](https://spacy.io/usage)

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(corrplot)
library(lme4)
library(mda.biber)
library(spacyr)
library(quanteda)
library(udpipe)
library(pseudobibeR)
```

## Intro

This pipeline describes the process of completing the MDA. See the [Santa Barbara Pipeline](santa_barbara_pipeline.md) and the [Scraps from the Loft Pipeline](scraps_from_loft_pipeline.md) for information on how the component data frames were assembled and where the data came from. 

This document is used to describe how the individual data frames were combined, the shape of the resulting data frame, and the steps of the analysis. Finally, it will briefly go over the results. If more details are needed to explain the steps of the MDA, see the [MDA document](mda.md). Final results and exploration of the analysis is documented in the [Dramaticity Analysis](final_report.md) document. 

## Creating all_transcripts DF

First, we load in the `tv_show_transcripts` pipeline as a csv.

```{r}
#| output: false

tv_show_df <- read.csv("private/tv_show_transcripts.csv")

tv_show_df
```


Then, we can load in the SB data frame. 

```{r}
#| output: false

sb_files <- read.csv("private/sb_files.csv")

sb_files
```

Finally, we combine the two data frames.

```{r}
#| output: false

all_transcripts <- rbind(sb_files, tv_show_df)

all_transcripts <- all_transcripts|>
  #renaming the first column to id and the second column to text as that is what is expected for the pseudobiber pipeline below
  rename(text = "clean_words",
         doc_id = "id")
```

Now we save this file to our private folder!

```{r}
write_csv(all_transcripts, "private/all_transcripts.csv")
```


## Summary `all_transcripts`

Below is some summary information about what is included in all_transcripts:

Number of rows and columns in our df and breakdown of genre

```{r}
nrow(all_transcripts)
ncol(all_transcripts)
all_transcripts |>
  mutate(doc_id = case_when(str_detect(doc_id, "trn") ~ "natural", 
                        str_detect(doc_id, "comedy") ~ "comedy", 
                        str_detect(doc_id, "drama") ~ "drama")) |>
  mutate(nwords = (str_count(text, "\\w+"))) |>
  count(doc_id)
```

Approximate number of words in our df:

```{r}
all_transcripts |>
  mutate(nwords = (str_count(text, "\\w+"))) |>
  summarize(sum(nwords))
```

Approximate number of words by category:

```{r}
all_transcripts |>
  mutate(doc_id = case_when(str_detect(doc_id, "trn") ~ "natural", 
                        str_detect(doc_id, "comedy") ~ "comedy", 
                        str_detect(doc_id, "drama") ~ "drama")) |>
  mutate(nwords = (str_count(text, "\\w+"))) |>
  group_by(doc_id) |>
  summarize(sum(nwords))
```


## Tagging all_transcripts and Getting Factor Loadings

In order to parse the data, it is necessary to use spaCy to tag all of the words in the document. Then, an R package called `pseudobibeR` can be used to get the 67 linguistic features created by Biber. For more details on the process, see [here](https://github.com/browndw/pseudobibeR). Note that this package and the following were created by David Brown, a linguist at CMU!

First, we can ensure that all texts are normalized and in a corpus format. A glimpse of the corpus format can be seen below.

```{r}
#| output: false

# 1. Read the texts and normalize typographic quotes (’ -> ')
all_transcripts$clean_words <- utf8::utf8_normalize(all_transcripts$clean_words, map_quote = TRUE)
corp <- corpus(all_transcripts)

corp
```
Next, we will download an English parsing model through `udpipe`. This is essentially a wrapper that allows R users to run tagging and parsing. 

```{r}
# 2. Parse with udpipe (the model is downloaded once)
model <- udpipe_download_model(language = "english")
```
Once the above code has been run once, only the below code will be necessary to load in the model as below. 

```{r}
ud_model <- udpipe_load_model(model$file_model)
```

And parse each character in the corpus. This process takes some time, around ten minutes. 

```{r}
parsed <- udpipe_annotate(ud_model, x = as.character(corp), doc_id = docnames(corp), trace = 100)
```
```{r}
parsed_df <- read_csv("private/parsed.csv")
```

Finally, we can get the feature weights which will be used in the second half of functions. This function also takes some time to run, about 2-3 minutes. 

```{r}
# 3. Count the features: one row per document
features <- biber(parsed)
```

```{r}
features <- read_csv("features.csv")
```


## Getting Dimension Scores

As can be seen in the `features` data structure, we have feature counts for each text. These can now be run through another series of functions to get the overall feature scores for the 67 linguistic features for each text and dimension scores. 

Once read in, the process described [here](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mda.biber/vignettes/introduction.html) is used to run our first attempt at the MDA. This is the second half of David Brown's pipeline!

Note that the documents are being renamed below such that each individual file is represented by it's category and no other information. For instance, each comedy TV show will only be known as comedy. This is necessary since we are comparing the groups as a whole.

```{r}
#| output: false

#ok so first we are assigning our data set to the variable d
d <- features |>
  #then, we are modifying a column called doc_id to rename columns that contain either "comedy", "drama" or "trn" with "comedy", "drama", and "natural". 
  mutate(doc_id = case_when(str_detect(doc_id, "comedy") ~ "comedy",
                            str_detect(doc_id, "drama") ~ "drama",
                            str_detect(doc_id, "trn") ~ "natural")) |>
  #then we are modifying our new column so the strings are factors
  mutate(doc_id = as.factor(doc_id)) |>
  #removes the columns with values = 0
  select(where(~ any(. != 0)))
```

This changes the labels of the id column so that our groups are formed, turns them into factors, and removes any columns with 0 instances. Any features not observed should not be there to run a proper mda as below.

## Determining Ideal Number of Factors

The next step in the analysis is to decide on how many factors should be formed from the factor loadings. See the [MDA](mda.md) document for more details on this important decision. 

```{r}
screeplot_mda(d)
```
A screeplot displays 'eigenvalues'. Simply put, it groups feature weights based on their impact on the data. Large feature loadings will therefore be grouped together, medium feature loadings grouped together, and so on. 

The 'elbow' is a term used to describe the cut off point where the features being grouped are not particularly impactful in terms of their predictive power. Visually, it is where the line becomes less steep. Anything at or below the elbow is considered 'scree'. 

In this case, we have decided to use the AF (accelerated factor) value to determine the elbow. This is a mathematical measure of where the line first begins to curve. Since there are two points above that, we should include two factors. Note that there is no easy way to determine the elbow or how many dimensions to include. If it is found that more dimensions might better suit an understanding of the data, re-analysis should be done.

In order to be sure that an MDA is worth running, we want to see that there is high correlation and inverse correlation among textual features. While this step is expected for textual features, it is still nice to run to be sure.

```{r}
cor_m <- cor(d[,-1], method = "pearson")

corrplot(cor_m, type = "upper", order = "hclust", tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45, diag = F, tl.cex = 0.5)
```
As we can see, there are multiple areas of dark blue (high correlation) and dark red (high inverse correlation). Therefore, we know that a multidimensional analysis makes sense for these groups. 

## Running the MDA

Next we are running the MDA. Essentially, we are getting mean scores for the significant feature loadings within each dimension (>.35).

```{r}
#now for the actual mda, factors is set equal to 2 because of the screeplot results
m <- mda_loadings(d, n_factors = 2)
```


And below we can see these mean values:

```{r}
dimension_scores <- attributes(m)$group_means

dimension_scores
```

Immediately, we can see a substantial difference between Factor 1 and Factor 2. While Drama scores quite distinctly from the other two groups in Factor 1, Natural language is quite different along Factor 2. A deeper analysis of the differences between these two factors will likely lead to a better understanding of where dramaticity comes into play. These differences can be even better visualized in graphic form.

Below are the highest correlation features by factor.

```{r}
#values arranged in descending order for factor 1
attributes(m)$loadings |> arrange(-Factor1)
```

```{r}
#values arranged in descending order for factor 1
#note that m contains the raw values while specifying loadings gets us the values normalized around 0
attributes(m)$loadings |> arrange(-Factor2)
```

If we consider Drama TV shows to generally have language that is more exaggerated compared to comedy TV shows and real life, then we could posit that dimension 1 is more likely to reflect the dimension of dramaticity. It is likely that dimension 2, then, more reflects differences between natural discourse and TV show discourse that are shared between the drama and comedy genre. A further analysis of the specific features involved will likely support this.

Given this hypothesis, for now we will focus on dimension 1.

```{r}
#mapping the mean dimension scores centered around 0
stickplot_mda(m, n_factor = 1)
```
This graph is a useful tool for understanding what the dimension analysis does. Based on the mean scores we saw earlier, the graph places all groups around 0. Since scores are averaged around 0, it is very easy to see how the different groups are on opposite ends of the spectrum for this dimension. 

```{r}
heatmap_mda(m, n_factor = 1)
```

By including the relevant features, things become even clearer. One important reminder is that highly positive and highly negative features (such as mean word length and adverbs) are in a trade off relationship. Among these groups, as the mean length of a word increases we would expect fewer adverbs to be present and vice versa. 

Two immediate thoughts based on this graph:

- it is suprising that emphatics are less likely to occur in drama TV show transcripts

- it is surprising that adverbs are also so unlikely in drama TV show transcripts

It will be important to sample some of the tags for these documents to better understand what is causing these rates. What sorts of words are being tagged as adverbs so frequently in the SB files?

## Linear Mixed Effect Model

A good next step in the analysis is to determine whether these groupings are significantly different along their dimensions. In other words, how well do the dimensions and their features predict a given group. 


## Defining Dimensions

In order to actually define our dimension, let's create two dfs. Each will depict the relevant linguistic features (positive and negative) in order of their significance or how strongly they seem to occur within the dimension. 

```{r}
loadings <- attributes(m)$loadings

#creating a new document of just the loadings
loadings
```

```{r}
#we have set our threshold at .35 or -.35 as is standard
threshold <- 0.35

# Dimension 1, taking only the factor 1 loadings above the absolute threshold
dim1_positive <- loadings[loadings$Factor1 >= threshold, ]
dim1_negative <- loadings[loadings$Factor1 <= -threshold, ]

# Dimension 2, taking only the factor 1 loadings above the absolute threshold
dim2_positive <- loadings[loadings$Factor2 >= threshold, ]
dim2_negative <- loadings[loadings$Factor2 <= -threshold, ]

#creating dimension 1 positive by itself with the factors in descending order
dim1_positive <- dim1_positive |>
  select(Factor1) |>
  arrange(desc(Factor1))

#creating dimension 1 negative by itself with the factors in ascending order
dim1_negative <- dim1_negative |>
  select(Factor1) |>
  arrange(Factor1)

#combine the vectors
dim1 <- dim1_positive |>
  rbind(dim1_negative)


#creating dimension 2 positive by itself with the factors in ascending order
dim2_positive <- dim2_positive |>
  select(Factor2) |>
  arrange(desc(Factor2))

#creating dimension 2 negative by itself with the factors in ascending order
dim2_negative <- dim2_negative |>
  select(Factor2) |>
  arrange(Factor2)

#combine the vectors
dim2 <- dim2_positive |>
  rbind(dim2_negative)

#results
dim1
dim2
```

### Dimension 1 - Should this incorporate other literature? Probably

Dimension 1 is slightly larger and is composed of 15 positive features and 13 negative ones. It is possible that this dimension is a bit overloaded (in the sense that it is trying to descirbe multiple underlying dimensions at the same time) which makes it more challenging to interpret. It groups Comedy and Natural discourse closer together on one end and Drama on the other.

Many of the positive features essentially boil down to higher information density. This fits in with Kozloff's idea that one key ways TV show dialogue differs from natural discourse is "communication of the narrative" (p. 33). Mean word length, prepositions, higher nouns overall (other nouns), nominalizations, agentless passives, and gerunds, which make up the five largest weights, all suggest that their texts are more focused on information and specificity (Biber 105-106). TTR and phrasal coordination, while less significant, also suggest this idea of more densely packed information with a need to express ideas faster. TTR could also be suggesting that natural discourse is more repetitive (or involved) which it likely is (`source`). This makes sense for the drama category as a genre distinction since often drama have more convoluted plots and need to communicate the narrative to viewers through dialogue (Kozloff). 

Elaborated explanation specific to verbal explanations: 
For verbal communication, several features have been considered methods for quickly expanding on information in a verbal context. Passed participle WHIZ and present participle whiz allow for elaboration on nouns more fluidly in conversation (Biber 105) and *that* in object position is similarly a way to elaborate on topics in conversation. The high use of these again suggests that drama particularly uses dialogue as a way to transfer information. 

Attributive adjectives

The above features could be considered a more practical, intuitive aspect of TV shows. Since they are constrained to a limited time frame and meant to be entertaining, they are often more information dense (`source`). While this could certainly contribute to the dialogue "sounding" more dramatic, some other features more suggest this notion. While less significant on this dimension (possible because comedy is closer on them). 



agentless passives, by passives, and verb suasives

As for the negative features, we have many that pattern straightforwardly as "high information." These include 

In conclusion, dimension 1 generally measures the different information loads that are being carried depending on the type of discourse being depicted. When looking at the average natural conversation (which varies greatly) we see a lower information density. Much of the space of language in conversation is taken up by repetitions, indexicalities, and stance taking. These features are usually not meant to convey meaning to an interlocutor that is not present (ie an audience). Drama, on the other hand, needs to move the plot forward. Comedy generally falls somewhere in between, but depending on the particular feature it can lean quite far away from natural discourse. Real natural discourse also shows clausal features that show more impromptu methods of elaboration. This suggests that this dimension also takes into acount methods of elaboration. 

So, dimension 1 can be described as: **high information and planned elaboration - low information and high indexicality/impromptu elaboration**

It makes sense, then, that comedy is grouped somewhat closer to drama. Comedy has been shown in Quaglio and Al-Surmi and other works to be close to natural discourse in a number of ways. And the plot of comedy generally requires less exposition through dialogue. And as a final reminder, this dimension is not as effective at dividing even drama from natural discourse. In part, that is because some (even many) forms of natural discourse will require high information and more planned elaboration. This dimension is less reliable.

### Dimension 2

Dramaticity

This dimension has much more promise to showcase those features that represent dramaticity. It is a smaller dimension made up of only 11 positive features and 9 negative ones. Natural discourse is grouped on the positive side while Comedy and Drama are grouped on the negative side. Already, this seems to suggest a dimension that is better dividing TV show discourse from Natural discourse.

Some of the positive features are repeated from dimension 1, suggesting that these are particularly potent features for creating an cline displaying natural-comedy-drama. These include contractions, negative analytics, demonstrative pronoun, and pronoun it. All of these suggest that for the dramas sampled, there is a specific and clear nature to the language compared with natural discourse. Contractions and negative synthetic elements are both easier to use with processing constraints such as in a real conversation (`source`). TV shows are pre-written and rehearsed, so these processing constraints are not an issue. And as mentioned at length in the first dimension, they want the audience to follow the dialogue easily. Demonstrative pronouns and pronoun it have lower weights but generally suggest the same differences above. Both are ways of quickly referring to things throughout the conversation, representing high interactivity. However for TV shows, high use of these functions can come off as repetitive or even dull (`source`). 

One overarching difference Quaglio focused on was that language is informal. For his comparison, he found the Friends was even *more* informal than natural discourse. However, a more complex finding here seems to be appearing. Features like discourse particles and stranded prepositions both co-occur positively with the positive side of dimension 2. These features are all marking some amount of informality. It is worth noting that many of the features in the previous paragraph could be grouped here. So, degree of informality seems to be one interpretation of the features so far. It is worth investigating why Quaglio's findings differed. One likely explanation is that due to a wider range of settings, there are simply too many TV shows in both comedy and drama that have reason to be more formal. Indeed, Friends could even be an outlier relative to the comedy genre in terms of informality. 

Third person pronouns and past tense could be associated with narrative language. Quaglio has an entire chapter devoted to differences in how narratives are portrayed in natural discourse versus television. Ultimately, both mediums make use of narratives, but natural discourse seems to use it more often. In this way, the findings of this dimension comparison seem to mirror findings by Quaglio. Story-telling is not prominent in either, but TV shows engage in it even less. Why is this? 

And lastly, for the positive features, we have clausal coordination, predictive modals, adverbial subordinators. These are all discourse features that show that natural discourse features more elaborations. In a TV show, lots of elaboration is somewhat reserved for special moments like monologues. For example, clausal coordinators, a very highly weighted feature, exemplifies how often people combine clauses using conjunctions in natural discourse. An easy way to clarify what you are saying, expand, and carry on conversation is to coordinate a new conjunction (`source`). Adverbial subordinators and predictive modals are very similar in this sense. 

For negative features, TTR and synthetic negatives contrast the first paragraph discussing positive features. They suggest that the texts within Drama and Comedy are less spontaneous or elaborated, which makes sense. 

Higher rates of both second and first persons pronouns and indefinite pronouns deserve some attention. This suggests a distinct difference in the manner of conversations happening in comedy and drama versus natural discourses. Basically, while natural discourses feature a bit more story telling and discussing of other people or discussion of the past, drama and comedy TV shows feature *a lot* more discussion of individuals within the conversation or discussion of people more generally. This could be because TV show characters are often "egotistical", they focus on themselves and those immediately around them. Indefinite pronouns specifically could also be a result of the common importance of tension coming from the unknown. For example in procedurals we often see conversations like "somebody died" or "anybody could have done it".

WH questions deserves it's own explanation. This feature has actually been found to be more frequent in TV show discourse before, and has been studied by Bednarek. Basically, it is well accounted that wh-questions are more common in TV show discourse. Why is this? This is one of those very cool linguistic characteristics that actually suggests dramaticity! In a TV show, questions create intrigue, explain the plot, raise the stakes, and create exciting dialogue.
NOTE -- Bednarek finds the most common trigrams for wh questions, this would be so cool to see for our corpus!!

Infinites are also somewhat difficult to place on their own. Similar to suasive verbs in dimension 1, they have been linked to persuasive elements in text. However, if it were about persuassion, we would expect to see more examples of other elements that suggest persuassion mixed in such as verb suasives and various types of modals. In fact, we see the opposite. Predictive modals are positive in dimension 2, meaning infinitives are in complementary distribution with them. Why then are infinitives found in dimension 2? From a more micro-analysis of the texts, it seems that infinitives occur more in drama (and to some extent comedy) because they are a means of expressing a character's internal desires or feelings. Expressions such as "want to" are particularly prevalant. 

Other nouns and mean word length have the smallest weight on the negative side for dimension 2. So, while we are still seeing some evidence of longer words and more nouns, it is not as evident as in dimension 1. Still, it is quite clear that comedy and drama both have slightly longer words on average and more nouns. As has been stated, this is likely a result of the higher information density of TV shows. 

In conclusion, Dimension 2 is closely related to Dimension 1 and there is certainly some cross-over. However, rather than a focus on information extent and methods of elaboration, it focuses more on the form the content takes and the sorts of structures required, namely more formality (contractions, stranded prepositions), character focus (wh-questions), and infrequent narrations. While narrative features are not common in any discourse (compared to, say, a novel), there is a clear division in which natural discourses engage in fairly frequent narratives but TV show dialogues restrict them to monologues and special moments (`source`). 

We could then describe this dimension as **informal/vague and relatively narrative to formal/clear and character driven**

## Deep Dive into Features

So, which features can be said to represent dramaticity? In a sense, all of them. While a distinction can be made (or indeed many distinctions) between the manner in which these features make a text *seem* more dramatic (what their function is within TV shows), those distinctions are debated in the literature and often depend on the particular show. A TV show that consists of friends talking over the dinner able versus one with doctors performing operations will obviously differ. However, the beauty of a multidimensional analysis which looks at various genres is that we can see broad patterns that still sneak through for any given TV show or natural discourse. 

Our two dimensions are currently:

**Dimension 1: high information and planned elaboration - low information and high indexicality/impromptu elaboration**

**Dimension 2: informal/vague and relatively narrative to formal/clear and character driven**

But another, less specific way of putting them would be:

**Dimension 1: Plot/Content heavy - Plot/Content light **

**Dimension 2: TV Show - Natural Discourse **

While this interpretation is not perfect, it lines up well with other literature. Quaglio examines 3 characteristics for which comedy is distant from Natural discourse: "Vague language, Emotional language, Informal Language, and Narrative language" (`source`). While Quaglio is only looking at one comedy and no TV shows from the drama genre, informality, vagueness, and narrativity were all present in Dimension 2 to some extent. Some of these did not match Quaglio's findings (notably formality), but that could be for a variety of reasons. From Kozloff's perspective, at least 3 features, "anchorage of the diegesis and characters," "character revelation," and "opportunities for 'star turns,'" are present to some extent in Dimension 2 as well (`source`). Additionally, wh-questions, explored by Bednarek, emerge as a prevelant feature. All of this suggests that Dimension 2 is stronger and matches findings from previous literature. 

It is time to dive into some specific examples to provide evidence for these dimensions and to explore which particular features may best showcase dramaticity. Based on a review of previous literature, the factor weights, and with a general preference for dimension 2, three categories have been created to explain how this dimension predicts a texts position. 

Interactivity and evidentiality:

- predictive modals

- clausal coordination

Character focus:

- Wh-questions

- first person pronouns

- infinitives

Narrativity:

- third person pronouns 

- past tense = narrative


To do this, we will need a data frame created from `parsed` from which we can find particular patterns, get examples, and create common pairings. Luckily, we have actually already done this! There is a very simple expression we can use to create a data frame from a udpipe which was accomplished above.

```{r}
parsed_df
```

Note that this is simply the spaCy tagging for every document. This is not the Biber tagging. In order to get Biber counts, we will have to find how the features were counted (often using a dict associated with Biber) and then search through `parsed_df`.

We will also need to reproduce word counts in order to normalize features to see meaningful total that line up with graphing `features`. 

Rough word count:

```{r}
word_counts <- parsed_df |>
  mutate(group = case_when(str_detect(doc_id, "trn") ~ "natural",
                            str_detect(doc_id, "comedy") ~ "comedy",
                            str_detect(doc_id, "drama") ~ "drama")) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(total_words = n(), .groups = "drop")

word_counts
```

### Interactivity 

#### Predictive Modals

To start, let's visualize what the counts say about the distribution of predictive modals in the data. 

```{r}
modal_pred <- features |> 
  #select doc_id and the relevant feature
  select(doc_id, f_54_modal_predictive) 

modal_pred

modal_pred_graph <- modal_pred |>
  #marge our 3 groups
  mutate(doc_id = case_when(str_detect(doc_id, "trn") ~ "natural",
                            str_detect(doc_id, "comedy") ~ "comedy",
                            str_detect(doc_id, "drama") ~ "drama")) 

ggplot(modal_pred_graph, aes(x = doc_id, y = f_54_modal_predictive, fill = doc_id)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Genre", y = "Count of Predictive Modals", title = "Predictive Modals") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Predictive Modals were one of the most highly weighted positive features within Dimension 2. From the graph above, we can see why. While natural discourse still has quite a spread, there is not very much overlap between groups. So, atural discourse uses predictive modals at a very high rate compared with either other genre. Why is this the case?

We can use our dictionary list to get a list of the lemmas and tags used to find and measure predictive modals. 

$f_54_modal_predictive
[1] "will_md"  "would_md" "shall_md" "'d_md"    "'ll_md"   "wo_md"    "sha_md" 

We can also search parsed_df to find what tag md refers to. 

```{r}
parsed_df
#first off, what is md?
unique(parsed_df$xpos)
```

Then, using parsed_df, we can search for the most common predictive modals for each text.

```{r}
pred_modal <- parsed_df |>
  #create categories again 
  mutate(group = case_when(str_detect(doc_id, "comedy") ~ "comedy",
                           str_detect(doc_id, "drama") ~ "drama",
                           str_detect(doc_id, "trn") ~ "natural")) |>
  #filter for modals tag
  filter(str_detect(xpos, "^(MD)"), 
         #filter for any of the accepted lemmas in the lemma column
         str_detect(lemma, "(will|would|shall|'d|'ll|wo|sha)")) |>
  #group by the category
  group_by(group) |>
  #count the lemma and name the column frequency
  count(lemma, name = "frequency") |>
  #put them in order of frequency and only take the most common 10
  slice_max(order_by = frequency, n = 10) 

pred_modal
```
Looking at the actual numbers, we see that 'would' and 'will' are the most important modals for determining these counts by far. To find out why this is the case, let's take a closer look at an example from each of our groups. 


```{r}
modal_examps <- parsed_df |>
  #create our groups
  mutate(group = case_when(str_detect(doc_id, "comedy") ~ "comedy",
                           str_detect(doc_id, "drama") ~ "drama",
                           str_detect(doc_id, "trn") ~ "natural")) |>
  #detect modals 
  filter(str_detect(xpos, "MD"),
         #detect predictive modals
         str_detect(lemma, "(will|would|shall|'d|'ll|wo|sha)")) |>
  #selects the main columns we want
  select(c(doc_id, sentence_id, sentence, token, lemma, upos, feats))


#normalized count
modal_count <- parsed_df |>
  mutate(group = case_when(str_detect(doc_id, "comedy") ~ "comedy",
                           str_detect(doc_id, "drama") ~ "drama",
                           str_detect(doc_id, "trn") ~ "natural")) |>
  filter(str_detect(xpos, "MD"),
         str_detect(lemma, "(will|would|shall|'d|'ll|wo|sha)")) |>
  group_by(group) |>
    summarise(modal_count = n(), .groups = "drop")
  
modal_count <- modal_count |>
  left_join(word_counts, by = "group") |>
  mutate(normalized = (modal_count / total_words) * 1000)

modal_count

modals_pitt_42_sheldon <- modal_examps |>
  #filter out only the 3 examples we want
  filter(doc_id == "the_pitt_drama" | doc_id == "trn_042" | doc_id == "young_sheldon_comedy") 

#raw count by word
modals_pitt_42_sheldon |>
  group_by(doc_id) |>
  count(lemma)
```

We can immediately see that our comedy example features far fewer 'will's and 'would's. The natural example and the drama example are actually quite close in their rates, in fact this time the drama is slightly higher overall. Why is this the case?

In the natural discourse, we see a lot of assertions through predictive modals.

TRN

KENDRA: Her mom **would** know. I'll have Melanie call you.

KITTY: Oh,

KENDRA:	Her mom call you,

KITTY:	right, right, her mom **wouldn't** lie

For example, in trn 42, we see a family argument. On 514, Kendra, the daughter, argues that her friend's mom would support her version of the story. This is in an attempt to convince her mom that she is telling the truth. In this way, it is often used as an argumentative style and one that is apparently extremely common in natural discourse. One reason might be that it is a softening of arguments we do not see as frequently in TV. 

The Pitt
SPEAKER 1: But you have to understand that **will** be the last test that we **would** do.

SPEAKER 2: If it comes back that there’s no blood flow to Nick’s brain, it **would** confirm beyond a shadow of a doubt that there’s been brain death, which **would** mean that he’s gone.

SPEAKER 1: Then we wait and see.

In the example from the Pitt, we see a similar example of discourse centered around assertions. In the example, the speakers are doctors trying to decide how to proceed with a patient. Since The Pitt is a medical procedure for which each season covers a single day, it makes sense that it would have frequent examples of individuals making assertions. 

Young Sheldon did not have any of these densely clustered predictive modals.

So, overall, we can say that as speakers try to express their points of view on events that occurred, they frequently use predictive modals as a tactic for convincing other interlocutors of their perspective. Why is this more frequent in natural discourse? I believe it is possible that since TV shows are generally less interactive than natural discourse, they make less use of features that are heavily utilized in interactive settings. When people talk in real life, it often centers on these kinds of arguments, soft back and forths in which people try to convince each other of things. In TV shows, while this strategy is certainly showcased, it is sparser than in natural discourse (in most cases). 


#### clausal coordination

Again, we will start with a visualization of clausal coordination. 

```{r}
clausal_coord <- features |> 
  select(doc_id, f_65_clausal_coordination) 

clausal_coord

clausal_coord_graph <- clausal_coord |>
  mutate(doc_id = case_when(str_detect(doc_id, "trn") ~ "natural",
                            str_detect(doc_id, "comedy") ~ "comedy",
                            str_detect(doc_id, "drama") ~ "drama")) |>
  arrange(doc_id)

ggplot(clausal_coord_graph, aes(x = doc_id, y = f_65_clausal_coordination, fill = doc_id)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Genre", y = "Count of Clausal Coordination", title = "Clausal Coordination") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
Here we see a distribution very similar to predictive modals. We can use similar tactics above to find only coordinating clauses. Though this time, it was a bit more complicated. In the [R documentation of the github for mda.biber](https://github.com/browndw/pseudobibeR/blob/main/R/parse_functions.R), we find the following code which was implemented for finding coordinated clauses. 

```
df[["f_65_clausal_coordination"]] <- tokens %>%
    dplyr::group_by(.data$doc_id) %>%
    dplyr::filter(
      .data$tag == "CC",
      .data$dep_rel != "ROOT",
      (
        dplyr::lead(.data$dep_rel == "nsubj") |
          dplyr::lead(.data$dep_rel == "nsubj", 2) |
          dplyr::lead(.data$dep_rel == "nsubj", 3)
      )
    ) %>%
    dplyr::tally() %>%
    dplyr::rename(f_65_clausal_coordination = "n")

```
Using this code, we can create a data frame made up of the coordinated conjunctions.

```{r}
clausal_coord <- parsed_df |>
  #get everything in the order the sentences should go in
  arrange(doc_id, sentence_id, token_id) |>
  #group by the categories
  group_by(doc_id) |>
  #find coordinating cunjunction tags
  filter(xpos == "CC",
         #exclude dependency relations not equal to root
         dep_rel != "root",
         (
           #lead basically finds following values so we can compare to make sure they're still subjects
           lead(dep_rel == "nsubj") |
           lead(dep_rel == "nsubj", 2) |
           lead(dep_rel == "nsubj", 3)
         )) |>
  mutate(group = case_when(str_detect(doc_id, "trn") ~ "natural",
                            str_detect(doc_id, "comedy") ~ "comedy",
                            str_detect(doc_id, "drama") ~ "drama")) 

#normalized counts
claus_count <- parsed_df |>
  arrange(doc_id, sentence_id, token_id) |>
  group_by(doc_id) |>
  filter(xpos == "CC",
         dep_rel != "root",
         (
           lead(dep_rel == "nsubj") |
           lead(dep_rel == "nsubj", 2) |
           lead(dep_rel == "nsubj", 3)
         )) |>
  mutate(group = case_when(str_detect(doc_id, "trn") ~ "natural",
                            str_detect(doc_id, "comedy") ~ "comedy",
                            str_detect(doc_id, "drama") ~ "drama")) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(claus_count = n(), .groups = "drop")

claus_count <- claus_count |>
  left_join(word_counts, by = "group") |>
  mutate(normalized = (claus_count / total_words) * 1000)

claus_count

#similar to above, we find 3 specific examples
clausal_white_sunny_31 <- clausal_coord |>
  filter(doc_id == "trn_031" | doc_id == "the_white_lotus_drama" | doc_id == "its_always_sunny_in_philadelphia_comedy")

#raw count
clausal_coord |>
  group_by(group) |>
  count()
```

Based on these numbers, natural discourse clearly uses clausal coordination to a greater extent on average. Let's look at some specific examples and consider why.

```{r}
clausal_white_sunny_31 |>
  group_by(doc_id) |>
  count(lemma)
```

Looks like these shows follow the overall trend very closely with comedy having the fewest clausal coordinators.

Natural:
SHERRY: She just has these little things that come every once in a while **and** they're always serious.

BETH: Why does she think she had a kidney infection.

ROSEMARY: Well she's got .. a pain, at .. at her waist, in the back, on one side only, **and** she's not, going to the bathroom as often as she should, even though she's drinking gallons of water,

We can immediately see that natural discourse frequently uses clausal coordinators simply to expand on thoughts and more thoroughly describe a situation. It is very easy to use coordinators to elaborate on points fluidly in conversation. 

We can see a similar pattern in the excerpts below. The coordinators are essentially being used for the same purpose. However, the distribution of these coordinators is very different. For TV shows, these pop up commonly in monologues, or at least lengthy segments of speech. In those cases, they serve their purpose: to highlight that the main speaker is elaborating on a subject. They might even serve especially well at this since we are conditioned to expect more information from these coordinators. For natural discourse, these kinds of elaborations pop up all over. 

Its Always Sunny in Philadelphia:
SPEAKER 1: My whole life, I thought I had shit for brains, mainly because my mom would stick a Tootsie Roll in my ear when I slept. **And** I would wake up and find it **and** I would think there was actually shit in my brains. Leaking out of your head at night? I think it’s because she loved me so much **and** she wanted to keep me at home, you know?

[Charlie] Sure, yeah.

SPEAKER 1: And then I wised up **and** I caught on to her love ruse, **and** I realized that I probably did have some kind of disorder."

The White Lotus:
SPEAKER 1: The room is– is beautiful, **and** we have this ocean view, **and** we face west, so we get these incredible sunsets.

SPEAKER 2: Yeah.

SPEAKER 1: You’d love Hawaii. Everything’s so lush. Where we are, it isn’t so overdeveloped. **And** there’s all of this amazing food and pastries."

#### Summary

Both clausal coordinators and predictive modals are examples of how TV shows utilize a sampling method to make dialogue *feel* interactive without feeling too repetitive. They can also use these features in particular situations to evoke specific emotions, a key feature of TV discourse (Kozloff). These features are quite similar in distribution between the drama and comedy genres.

### Character Focus

#### WH Questions

```{r}
wh <- features |> 
  select(doc_id, f_13_wh_question) 

wh

wh_graph <- wh |>
  mutate(doc_id = case_when(str_detect(doc_id, "trn") ~ "natural",

                            str_detect(doc_id, "drama") ~ "drama")) |>

ggplot(wh_graph, aes(x = doc_id, y = f_13_wh_question, fill = doc_id)) +

  labs(x = "Genre", y = "Count of WH Questions", title = "WH Questions") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
WH Questions are most common in the comedy genre followed by drama, and finally natural discourse. The frequency of WH Questions in TV shows has actually been examined at length and this finding is yet another example of this trend. Let's explore why this occurs through specific examples in the corpus.

```{r}
wh_count

#similar to above, we find 3 specific examples
wh_trn_057 <- wh_questions |>
  filter(doc_id == "trn_057" | doc_id == "beauty_in_black_drama" | doc_id == "curb_your_enthusiasm_comedy")

wh_questions |>
```

In this case, our raw counts differ from the normalized trend. By looking at the numbers normalized per thousand, we see the trend from the graph above. Let's take a look at our specific examples.

```{r}
wh_trn_057 |>
  filter(doc_id == "trn_057" | doc_id == "beauty_in_black_drama" | doc_id == "curb_your_enthusiasm_comedy") |>
  group_by(doc_id) |>
  count(lemma)

wh_trn_057
```

These results are quite shocking! Admittedly, these are TV shows with *particularly* high counts, but the trend holds true for many of the TV shows. Why is this the case? 

In the natural discourse below, Nick is a judo instructor. He is trying to teach his students a new throw. His question at the end is rhetorical, and likely meant to encourage the student to try the throw. In natural discourse, these kinds of rhetorical questions are not as common as simple fact seeking questions (`source`). 

Natural:
NICK: Now I'm gonna be a sucker, and watch your feet. This- Now you're just walking in on me man, you have- you have no outer winding pull here. Jerk me to you. Hoo, there we go, I'm on my tiptoes, what are you waiting for.

In the discourse below, Horace and Kimmie are having an argument about the status of their relationship. Almost immediately after Kimmie storms off, Angel asks her what she was doing in Horace's room. This is a prime example of how TV can use wh-questions for "expression of emotion/opinion" (Kimmie's line shows that she is confused and upset by Horace's aloofness) and to progress the narrative in an exciting way (Angel's immediate interest in what Kimmie was doing) (Bednarek, 2014a). 

Beauty in Black:
KIMMIE: Look… [scoffs] **What**… what the hell am I missing here?

HORACE: Kimmie.

ANGEL: **What** were you doing in there? 

KIMMIE: Mind your business.

Based on the overall counts, this also seems to be slightly more common in comedies than either other group. This matches Quaglio's finding that Friends featured a lot of language used to express emotions, which wh-questions are certainly very capable of doing (`Quaglio`).

```{r}
first_019_last_adults
```

Ok, we can see from these results that the most common pronoun is 'I' by far. Next, 'we' for all of the groups with 'my' being a sometimes close second. All other pronouns look surprisingly rare. Starting with drama and comedy, an explanation for the greater number of first person pronouns can be found when considering the main topic of TV shows: the characters. TV shows are largely about the characters they depict (`source?`). First person pronouns are a primary way for characters to make observations, statements, and emotional expressions within the dialogue. 'We' is so prominent in this episode of The Last of Us, for instance, because it is largely about a couple discussing their lives and their relationship during an apocalypse. 

This scene depicts the characters trying to grapple with what their lives are going to be like. Bill asks a rhetorical question in 883 as he believes there is no reason for them to have dinner parties. Frank replies, redefining his expectation of their life as having friends in 887 and expands on his views in 891. Finally Bill counters again, saying their lives cannot be that way in 892 and 894. Ultimately, the pronoun 'we' has come to represent their life in a natural, engaging way for the audience. 

The Last of Us
BILL: Are-are **we** hosting formal garden parties now?

FRANK: No.

FRANK: But **we** are gonna have friends.

BILL: Excuse me?

FRANK: **We**’re gonna make friends, and **we** will invite them to visit.

BILL: **We** don’t have friends, Frank.

BILL: **We** will never have friends because there are no friends to be had.


Adults:
ANTON: No, you let him pee through your legs? 

ISSA: All the time.

ANTON: We call it “log fluming” ’cause she’s usually dropping one…

PAUL: Anton, just go downstairs! 

The Adults transcript showcases another use of first person pronouns, that they can also create humor and show the connections between characters. Here, Anton's use of 'we' is suggesting both that Issa and Anton are quite close (to be willing to log flume) and creates a humorous encounter for the audience. 

To be clear, the natural discourse still features lots of personal pronouns. However, they appear to be more intermittent and to be used in more practical ways like discussing plans for the group. 

Natural:
SPEAKER 1: Are we going to that?

SPEAKER 2: Yes.


While natural discourse is clearly not lacking in personal pronouns, TV show dialogues have reason to lean more heavily into their use. More space in TV show dialogue is given to explaining positions and emotions very explicitly because it is easier for the audience to engage in (`source`).

#### Summary

WH questions, first person pronouns, and infinitives are all linguistic markers that seem to co-occur more often in a text in order to focus more on characters and their emotional states. Since drama and comedy genres revolve around the characters and their stories, all three features are on average more likely to occur in these groups.

As for a difference between genres, we see that characters expressing their emotions/opinions appears to be generally more common in the comedy genre. Quaglio explores this in a chapter and demonstrates that Friends contains more emotional language than natural discourse. This finding does not hold for infinitives, which may be a reason to explore more functions infinitives might be serving in the different groups. Drama otherwise seems to vary more often, suggesting that the emphasis on emotional expression probably depends on what exactly the drama is about. Almost all TV shows in the comedy genre have a heavy focus on the interpersonal relationships between the characters. For drama, this may vary more often.


### Narrativity

For the last category of narrativity, we will explore both past tense and third person pronouns in conjunction. We want to find text examples of narratives to explore how they are used relative to each other.

```{r}
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Seeing these two graphs side by side, it seems very clear that there is a pattern here with narratives being more common in natural discourse. Intuitively, this might seem opposite of what is expected. After all, if TV shows are about story telling, shouldn't there be a lot fo narratives? Let's take a closer look. 
$f_01_past_tense
[1] "*_vbd"

$f_08_third_person_pronouns
[1] "she_prp*"        "he_prp*"         "they_prp*"       "her_prp*"        "him_prp*"       
 [6] "them_prp*"       "his_prp*"        "their_prp*"      "himself_prp*"    "herself_prp*"   
[11] "themselves_prp*"

str_detect()
str_detect(lemma, "(she|he|they|her|him|them|his|their|himself|herself|themselves)")

 filter(str_detect(xpos, "^W") == T,
       upos != "DET" & lead(dep_rel == "aux"),
      (lag(upos == "PUNCT", default = T) |
          lag(upos == "PUNCT", 2, default = T))) |>

```{r}
#finding all past tense verbs that are either preceded or followed by a third person pronoun
past_third_pers <- parsed_df |>
  mutate(group = case_when(str_detect(doc_id, "comedy") ~ "comedy",
                           str_detect(doc_id, "drama") ~ "drama",
                           str_detect(doc_id, "trn") ~ "natural")) |>
  filter(str_detect(xpos, "VBD"),
         !is.na(lemma),
         (lag(xpos == "PRP") & lag(str_detect(lemma, "(she|he|they|her|him|them|his|their|himself|herself|themselves)"))) |
           lead(xpos == "PRP") & lead(str_detect(lemma, "(she|he|they|her|him|them|his|their|himself|herself|themselves)"))
         ) |>
  select(c(doc_id, sentence_id, sentence, token, lemma, upos, feats, group))

past_third_pers

#count of sentences with past tense and a third person pronoun
past_third_pers |>
  group_by(group) |>
  count()

#specific examples
past_third_37_lucifer_scrubs <- past_third_pers |>
  #filter out only the 3 examples we want
  filter(doc_id == "trn_037" | doc_id == "lucifer_drama" | doc_id == "scrubs_2026_comedy") 
```

It is convenient to look at these features side by side because past tense and third person pronouns are strong indicators of narratives in stories. Since these have been shown by Quaglio to be one of the differences between TV show discourse and natural discourse, it is worth taking a close look at.

```{r}
past_third_37_lucifer_scrubs
```

Here we see a mini-narrative from the natural discourse. The woman is talking about Willy as a boy and a time that he took some uncooked tamales. These kinds of narratives are far more common in natural discourse (`Quaglio`). Telling stories of course does occur in TV show dialogue, but it is generally used as some kind of character moment to explain back story. As an alternative, character back story in TV shows can be explained through a flash back which does not require these story telling features. 

Natural:
SPEAKER: Tina always makes some tamales? And when Willy was a little boy, **he saw** that, **she had** a lot of tamales already. Uh, in the shop, and and in the meat and everything? And **he got** some and, went out the house? And **they were** not cook.

Lucifer:
SPEAKER: Everyone thought **he died** of a heart attack, but Ella figured out he was murdered.

Scrubs:
SPEAKER: Like my dad, when **he told** me my dog, Puddles, had been “discovered” and was moving to Hollywood. I watched 88 dog films over the course of 13 years till one day my dad finally admitted that Puddles had to be put to sleep when **he bit** our neighbor.

Drama and comedy do not have as many of these continued narratives. In Lucifer, for example, this line stands alone as a brief reminder of a plot point for the audience. In the comedy example, we see something closer to a mini narrative. However, we can see from the overall graphs that these mini-narratives (or even longer narratives) are relatively rare in comedy. 


#### Summary

Overall, this again suggests that because comedy and drama generally focus on what the characters are currently doing and their conversations are more focused one establishing their internal feelings and perspectives, we do not get the same quantity of stories. As a result, one key part of dramaticity could be said to be an increased focus on the characters in the present moment. In natural discourse, people spend a lot fo time reminiscing, sharing connections through stories (`source`). 

Comedy features even fewer of these. Characters in sit coms are notoriously egotistical. Additionally, the trope of a character in a drama telling a heartfelt story that reveals aspects of their personality is well-documented (`source`).
